results.title: What are the differences between ZCU102, ZCU104 and ZCU106?
results.content:
Title: What are the differences between ZCU102, ZCU104 and ZCU106?
The big downside of the ZCU104 is the lack of high-speed connectivity. The ZCU102 has 16 GTH transceivers on the FMC ports, plus four on SFP, plus GTRs on the PCIe slot. The ZCU106 has 7 GTHs on FMC, plus two on SFP, plus four on PCIe, plus one on SMA connectors. one GTH on FMC, and no other general-purpose high-speed transceivers (only those that are used for SATA, USB3.0, DisplayPort, HDMI, etc). For anyone looking at doing high-speed connections to embedded hardware - for example to a very high-speed camera sensor IC, or to other FPGAs - the ZCU104 is unsuitable. On the other hand, if you're designing a small system that'll use SATA, USB3.0, ethernet, and HDMI/DisplayPort as its interfaces, the ZCU104 is fantastic. If you're experimenting with hardware acceleration (ignoring the interfaces) then the ZCU104 is probably pretty good - although being able to plug the ZCU106 into a PCIe slot is nice too. Title: Reducing the resource utilization , and convert LUT memory to BRAM
Reducing the resource utilization , and convert LUT memory to BRAM. i want to reduce the resource utilization on Zynq-7020, now its 85% of LUT's utilizing want to reduce it to less than 60%, and cant make any changes in RTL, Because its tool generated RTL. and any possibility to convert LUT memory to BRAM in tool options. Check if RAM\_STYLE attribute on cells helps in converting them to BRAM:. https://www.xilinx.com/support/documentation/sw\_manuals/xilinx2018\_2/ug912-vivado-properties.pdf#page=314. https://support.xilinx.com/s/question/0D52E00006hpbesSAA. – This thread was edited to update links as a result of our community migration. In general, converting LUT RAM to BRAM is not possible. BRAM is much slower (because data has to be routed to/from the BRAM tiles), it has an absolute minimum of 1-cycle latency (LUT RAM can do combinational), and it cannot have more than two ports (LUT RAM can have four ports). As a result, I wouldn't count on Vivado being able to automatically convert LUT RAM to block RAM in most cases. One of the things that really take up resources in many Zynq designs is bus converters. I have seen designs using a lot of AXI to AXI-lite converters that really wasn't necessary. If you can do with AXI-lite then just use one converter and use an expander to connect all your AXI-lite IP to this. results.title: ChatGPT's energy use per query | Towards Data Science
results.content: Another reason why it’s interesting to look into ChatGPT’s energy use per query is that it’ll enable individuals to come up with their own estimates of ChatGPT’s total electricity consumption or carbon footprint. Now, let’s apply these methods to produce estimates of ChatGPT’s energy use per query. In this section, I’ll present the estimates of how much energy ChatGPT needs to answer one request, along with the measured energy consumption per query of two other large language models, BLOOM and GPT-J, as reported elsewhere [9][10]. In Table 1 below, we can see that method 1 and 2 yield similar estimates of ChatGPT’s energy consumption per query. Using method 1, ChatGPT’s estimated energy consumption per query is 0.0017 KWh at the lower range (average power draw is 50 % of TDP) and 0.0026 at the higher range (average power draw is 75 % of TDP). Using method 2, ChatGPT’s estimated energy use per request is 0.0018 KWh. Table 1: ChatGPT's estimated energy use per query. Let’s see how the estimates of ChatGPT’s electricty use per query compare to the electricty use per query observed for other LLMs. Table 2 below shows the energy consumption per query for GPT-J and BLOOM. Notice that BLOOM’s electricity consumption per query is not much larger than the estimated electricity consumption per query for ChatGPT, while GPT-J’s energy use is noticeably larger. ![Table 2: Comparing the estimated electricity consumption per query for ChatGPT to the measured electricity consumption per query for BLOOM and GPT-J reported in [9][10]](). Also note that the estimated quantity is the *average* electricity consumption of a ChatGPT query because we use Microsoft’s *average* PUE. If you’d like to estimate *your* electricity consumption from using ChatGPT or similar services, you should use the PUE of the data center you expect handles your requests. This blog post estimates that ChatGPT’s energy use per request is smaller than the measured energy consumption of the LLM called BLOOM. On AI stack exchange [7], Mike Ellis has calculated ChatGPT’s energy consumption using method 2 and arrived at 0.000083 KWh per query. This article estimates that ChatGPT may use between 0.0017 and 0.0026 KWh of electricity to answer one query.
